library(reticulate)

Wikipedia pages where the data is a bulleted list or a category rather than a table. These need a different scraping method than `pandas.read_html()`.

* [Category:Defunct shopping malls in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Defunct_shopping_malls_in_the_United_States): no "List of" article exists for closed malls, so this category is the closest substitute, with [Demolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Demolished_shopping_malls_in_the_United_States) and [Abandoned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Abandoned_shopping_malls_in_the_United_States) subcategories.
* [List of defunct department stores of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_defunct_department_stores_of_the_United_States): bulleted by state, with store name, location, and closure notes. The entries need manual structuring into columns.
* [Timeline of malware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_malware): a chronological bulleted list grouped by decade, then year. Covers ILOVEYOU, Melissa, and Code Red.
* [List of companies affected by the dot-com bubble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_companies_affected_by_the_dot-com_bubble): a bulleted list of companies, each with a prose description of its IPO, stock performance, or collapse.

## Scraping method

A Wikipedia category has no table, it is just a list of page links, so `pandas.read_html()` has nothing to parse. The MediaWiki API's `categorymembers` endpoint returns the same list as structured JSON instead, and handles pagination with a `cmcontinue` token for categories over 500 members.

This fetches the defunct malls category and its two subcategories, and labels each page with the category it came from.

```{python}
#| label: scrape-malls
#| eval: false
import pandas as pd
import requests

API = "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php"

def fetch_category_members(category):
    params = {
        "action": "query", "list": "categorymembers",
        "cmtitle": f"Category:{category}", "cmlimit": 500,
        "format": "json"
    }
    members = []
    while True:
        resp = requests.get(API, params=params, headers={"User-Agent": "wikimill-project/0.1"}).json()
        members.extend(resp["query"]["categorymembers"])
        if "continue" not in resp:
            break
        params["cmcontinue"] = resp["continue"]["cmcontinue"]
    return pd.DataFrame(members)[["title"]]

categories = {
    "Defunct_shopping_malls_in_the_United_States": "Defunct",
    "Demolished_shopping_malls_in_the_United_States": "Demolished",
    "Abandoned_shopping_malls_in_the_United_States": "Abandoned",
}
malls = pd.concat(
    [fetch_category_members(cat).assign(status=label) for cat, label in categories.items()],
    ignore_index=True
)
malls.to_csv("data/defunct_malls.csv", index=False)
malls.head()
```

This chunk is shown for reference only (`eval: false`), rendering the site doesn't hit Wikipedia. Run `python src/scrape_malls.py` from the project root to refresh `data/defunct_malls.csv`.

## Data manipulation in R

A mall in the "Demolished" or "Abandoned" subcategory is also a member of the parent "Defunct" category, so each title can appear more than once. This keeps the most specific status per mall and counts how many fall into each one.

```{r}
#| label: clean-malls
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(forcats)

malls_clean <- read_csv("data/defunct_malls.csv") |>
  mutate(status = factor(status, levels = c("Demolished", "Abandoned", "Defunct"))) |>
  arrange(status) |>
  distinct(title, .keep_all = TRUE)

write_csv(malls_clean, "data/defunct_malls_clean.csv")

malls_clean |> count(status, sort = TRUE)
```
